title: SHE WAS USED, MISTREATED, AND LEFT TO DIE IN THE WILDERNESS—BUT GOD CALLED HER BY NAME
paragraphs: SHE WAS USED, MISTREATED, AND LEFT TO DIE IN THE WILDERNESS—BUT GOD CALLED HER BY NAME
The heartbreaking story of Hagar, the Egyptian servant who bore Abraham’s first son, and the God who saw a woman everyone else treated as disposable. — Genesis 16:1–16
She was not the woman who received the promise.
She was not the wife whose name would become famous.
She was not the one who made the decision.
But she was the one who had to carry the consequences.
And somewhere in the wilderness, pregnant, frightened, and running from the household that had wounded her, an Egyptian servant experienced something extraordinary.
The God of Abraham came looking for her.
Not because she was powerful.
Not because she had a respectable position.
Not because she had everything figured out.
But because the God who rules heaven and earth does not overlook the suffering of people the world has learned to ignore.
Her name was Hagar.

And if you have ever felt used by someone you trusted, blamed for a situation you never created, or forgotten while everyone else moved forward with their lives, you may discover something deeply personal in her story.
Because before Hagar ever called God the One who sees her, God had already seen everything.
And what happened next would echo through generations.
Genesis 16 begins inside a household that should have been overflowing with faith.

God had promised Abram descendants. He had called him out of his homeland and promised that his offspring would become a great nation. In Genesis 15:5, God had even pointed Abram toward the stars, declaring that his descendants would be beyond counting.
But years were passing.
Sarai remained childless.
And waiting was becoming painful.
There is a kind of waiting that slowly exhausts the human heart.
You pray.
You believe.
You remind yourself of what God has said.
Then another year passes, and nothing seems to change.
Eventually, the temptation comes to do something—anything—to make the promise happen.
That is where the trouble began.
Genesis 16:1 introduces a woman who had little control over what would happen next:
“Now Sarai Abram's wife bare him no children: and she had an handmaid, an Egyptian, whose name was Hagar.”
— Genesis 16:1, KJV
Notice how Scripture introduces her.
An Egyptian.
A servant.
A woman belonging to Sarai's household.
Her name was Hagar, but her social position defined how others could treat her.
The Hebrew word translated “handmaid” is שִׁפְחָה (shiphchah), a term referring to a female servant or enslaved woman.
This was not simply a modern employment arrangement.
Hagar lived within a household structure in which she had far less power than Abram and Sarai.
And that matters.
Because when we read what happened next, we must not imagine three equally powerful adults making an ordinary family decision.
Sarai had a plan.
Since she had not conceived, she proposed that Abram have a child through Hagar.
In the ancient Near Eastern world, arrangements involving enslaved women and childbearing were known. But something being culturally practiced does not mean God commanded or approved it.
Genesis records Sarai's proposal.
It does not present her proposal as a divine instruction.
And Abram agreed.
The man who had received God's promise listened to a human plan that would bring tremendous pain into his household.
Hagar conceived.
And suddenly, the woman who had been treated as a means to someone else's desired future became the center of a bitter conflict.
Genesis 16:4 tells us that when Hagar realized she was pregnant, her mistress became despised in her eyes.
Scripture does not conceal Hagar's response.
She was not portrayed as morally flawless.
But neither does her response erase the enormous imbalance of power surrounding her.
Sarai became angry.
She blamed Abram.
Abram then placed Hagar back under Sarai's authority.
And Genesis 16:6 records the devastating result:
“And when Sarai dealt hardly with her, she fled from her face.”
The Hebrew verb behind “dealt hardly” comes from עָנָה (anah), which in this context conveys harsh treatment or affliction.
It was serious enough that Hagar ran away.
Pregnant.
Alone.
Without the security of a household.
Heading into the wilderness.
Think about that for a moment.
The child she carried was Abram's son.
Yet she was the one fleeing.
The powerful remained inside their tents.
The vulnerable woman was outside, facing the uncertainty of the desert.
Sometimes the people who should have protected you become the very people whose presence you fear.
Sometimes you suffer because of decisions made by people with more authority than you.
Sometimes you are expected to carry pain quietly because telling the truth would make everyone uncomfortable.
And sometimes the deepest wound is not simply what happened.
It is the terrible suspicion that nobody cares.
But Hagar's story did not end with her running away.
It continued with God finding her.
Genesis 16:7 says:
“And the angel of the LORD found her by a fountain of water in the wilderness, by the fountain in the way to Shur.”
The Hebrew expression is מַלְאַךְ יְהוָה (mal'akh YHWH), meaning “the angel of the LORD” or “the messenger of the LORD.”
This is a remarkable encounter.

The passage describes the messenger speaking with divine authority, and Hagar later identifies the LORD as the One who spoke to her. Christians have understood the identity of the angel of the LORD in different ways; some see a manifestation of God, while others understand a divine messenger representing Him.
The text itself makes the central truth unmistakable.
The LORD was not unaware of Hagar's suffering.
The messenger found her.
That word matters.
Hagar did not arrange a meeting.
She did not have a sanctuary, a priest, or a position of religious influence.
She was a runaway Egyptian servant beside a spring.
And heaven had not lost sight of her.
Then came a question.
“Hagar, Sarai's maid, whence camest thou? and whither wilt thou go?”
— Genesis 16:8, KJV
He called her Hagar.
By name.
Not merely Abram's servant.
Not merely Sarai's property.
Not merely the woman carrying someone else's child.
Hagar.
God knew who she was.
And the question was piercing.
Where have you come from?
Where are you going?
She knew where she had come from.
“I flee from the face of my mistress Sarai.”
But Scripture does not record her answering where she was going.
Perhaps she did not know.
Perhaps escaping the pain had become more urgent than knowing the destination.
Have you ever lived through a season like that?
You knew what had hurt you.
You knew what you could no longer endure.
But you had no idea what tomorrow would look like.
You were surviving one day at a time.
And underneath all the brave words, you were wondering whether God could still see you.
Hagar's encounter answers that question in a way no human reassurance could.
Yet the next part of the story is difficult.
The angel instructed Hagar to return to Sarai and submit to her authority.
We should not soften this verse or pretend it is easy.
Nor should we misuse it.
Genesis 16:9 is not a universal command for abused people to return to dangerous situations.
It records a specific instruction given to Hagar in a particular encounter with God. It must never be used to pressure someone to remain in violence, exploitation, or abuse.
The Bible's account of what God told Hagar is not permission for anyone today to mistreat another human being.
And the instruction was accompanied by a promise.
God declared that Hagar's descendants would become too numerous to count.
Then the angel said:
“Behold, thou art with child, and shalt bear a son, and shalt call his name Ishmael; because the LORD hath heard thy affliction.”
— Genesis 16:11, KJV
Ishmael.
In Hebrew, יִשְׁמָעֵאל (Yishma'el) means “God hears” or “God will hear.”
The explanation in Genesis 16:11 connects his name directly to the LORD hearing Hagar's affliction.
Pause there.
The woman who had been treated as though her suffering did not matter was told to give her son a name that would testify to God's hearing.
Every time she called him, she would be reminded of the wilderness.
Of the spring.
Of the voice.
Of the God who heard her pain.
The child was not an accident outside God's knowledge.
He was not the promised covenant heir through whom the particular promise to Abraham and Sarah would be fulfilled—that role would belong to Isaac, as Genesis 17:19–21 later makes clear.
But Ishmael was not forgotten by God.
The Lord promised him descendants.
God's covenant purposes through Isaac did not cancel His compassion toward Hagar and Ishmael.
And that distinction is important.
God's promises are not interchangeable, but His mercy is not restricted to the people we consider most important.
The passage also foretells that Ishmael's life and relationships would be marked by conflict and independence. Genesis 16:12 is not a sentimental promise that every hardship would disappear.
God did not tell Hagar that the road ahead would be effortless.
He told her that He had heard.
And sometimes that is the beginning of a faith that can endure what it cannot yet understand.
Then comes one of the most beautiful moments in Genesis.
Hagar responds to the LORD who spoke to her.
Genesis 16:13 says:
“And she called the name of the LORD that spake unto her, Thou God seest me.”
The Hebrew expression is אֵל רֳאִי (El Ro'i), commonly understood as “God who sees me” or “God of seeing.”

The Hebrew wording of the verse contains interpretive difficulties, and translations differ in how they render Hagar's explanation. But the connection between God and His seeing of Hagar is central to the passage.
Imagine the weight of that confession.
A woman whose life had been controlled by other people was now speaking about God from her own encounter with Him.
She had been seen.
Not merely noticed from a distance.
Not observed with cold indifference.
Seen by the LORD who knew her name, her circumstances, and the child inside her womb.
El Ro'i.
The God who sees me.
Not just the God who sees kings.
Not just the God who sees prophets.
Not just the God who sees the people whose names appear in genealogies and promises.
The God who sees the exhausted.
The frightened.
The overlooked.
The person whose tears have become so familiar that nobody asks about them anymore.
And perhaps that is where this ancient story reaches into your life.
Because there are people reading this who know what it feels like to be surrounded by others and still feel invisible.
You have become the dependable one.
The strong one.
The person who keeps the family together.
The person who serves at church even when your own heart is tired.
The person who encourages everyone else while privately wondering who will encourage you.
You smile in photographs.
You answer, “I'm fine.”
You post a Bible verse.
Then the room gets quiet, and the pain returns.
You wonder whether your prayers are reaching heaven.
Whether the years you have spent waiting have meant anything.
Whether your mistakes have disqualified you from being loved.
Whether God has moved on to people who seem more faithful, more successful, more spiritually impressive.
Hagar's story does not promise that every problem will disappear tomorrow.
It tells you something deeper.
Your suffering is not hidden from God.
And that truth becomes even more powerful when we follow the story of Scripture toward Jesus Christ.
Centuries after Hagar stood beside a wilderness spring, the Son of God entered a world filled with people who were overlooked, rejected, and burdened.
Jesus saw a Samaritan woman at a well whose complicated history had not escaped Him (John 4).
He saw a woman suffering from bleeding for twelve years, whose desperate touch was lost in the movement of a crowd until He stopped and spoke to her (Mark 5:25–34).
He saw Zacchaeus in a tree, a despised tax collector whom others had already judged (Luke 19:1–10).
He saw a widow grieving her only son and responded with compassion (Luke 7:11–15).
Again and again, Jesus revealed that people are not disposable to God.
And then He went to the cross.
Not merely to make wounded people feel noticed.
But to accomplish something infinitely greater.
To bear sin.
To reconcile sinners to God.
To open the way for forgiveness, repentance, and new life.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
This is the heart of the Gospel.
Jesus does not simply affirm everything we have done.
He calls us to repent.
He does not pretend sin is harmless.
He died because sin is deadly.
He does not offer healing by denying the truth.
He offers grace that brings the truth into the light and transforms those who trust Him.
And this is where we must be careful not to turn Hagar's story into something Scripture never intended.
Hagar was not saved by becoming important in the eyes of the world.
Her encounter was not proof that every human plan would succeed.
Her story was not a promise that God would immediately remove every consequence of human failure.
It was a revelation of divine compassion in the middle of a broken household.
And the fuller biblical revelation points us to Jesus Christ, in whom God's mercy and saving purpose are made known.
The same Bible that records Hagar's tears also reveals the Savior who came to rescue sinners.
A Savior who knows what rejection feels like.
A Savior who was betrayed.
A Savior who was falsely accused.
A Savior who suffered at the hands of sinful people.
A Savior who did not remain in the grave.
Jesus Christ rose again.
And because He lives, our deepest hope is not that we can somehow rewrite our own past.
It is that the risen Christ can redeem people whose past cannot be undone.
That does not make every wrong thing good.
It means evil and human failure do not have the final authority over God's redemptive purposes.
And there is another part of Hagar's story we cannot ignore.
She returned.
Genesis 16 concludes with the birth of Ishmael.
Abram was eighty-six years old when Ishmael was born.
The child received the name God had announced.
The servant who had fled into the wilderness became the mother of Abraham's first son.
But her story did not end there.
Years later, after Isaac was born, Hagar and Ishmael would face another devastating departure from Abraham's household.
Genesis 21 records Hagar wandering in the wilderness of Beersheba, her water exhausted, unable to bear the thought of watching her son die.
She wept.
And once again, God intervened.
Genesis 21:17 says that God heard the voice of the boy.
Then God opened Hagar's eyes, and she saw a well of water.
Do you see the recurring testimony?
In Genesis 16, God heard her affliction.
In Genesis 21, God heard the boy.
The family conflict was real.
The consequences were real.
The wilderness was real.
But God's attention had not vanished.
He had not forgotten the mother or her child.
And this is something you may need to hear today.
Just because God met you in one difficult season does not mean you will never experience another.
Just because you have prayed sincerely does not mean you will never cry again.
Just because you belong to Christ does not mean life will never hurt.
But the faithfulness of God is not measured by how quickly every hardship disappears.
It is revealed in His character, His promises, and ultimately in the finished work of Jesus Christ.
Perhaps your wilderness is not a desert.
Perhaps it is a marriage filled with silence.
A hospital corridor.
An empty bank account.
A strained relationship with your child.
A private battle with temptation.
A season of shame after a sin you desperately wish you could undo.
Perhaps you have been wounded by people who speak about God but have failed to treat you with His compassion.
Or perhaps, painfully, you recognize yourself not only in Hagar's suffering but also in Sarai's impatience or Abram's failure to act rightly.
Maybe you have tried to force an outcome because waiting on God felt unbearable.
Maybe you have hurt someone while trying to protect your own dream.
Maybe you have justified behavior you knew was wrong because you were afraid of losing control.
Then this story is not only an invitation to receive comfort.
It is an invitation to examine your heart.
Because the Gospel does not merely tell the wounded that God sees them.
It calls the proud to humility.
The unjust to repentance.
The fearful to trust.
The sinner to the Savior.
And the believer to walk in a new way.
If you have mistreated someone, do not use God's grace as an excuse to avoid responsibility.
Repent.
Tell the truth.
Seek to make things right where possible.
If you have been mistreated, do not confuse forgiveness with pretending that harm never happened.
God's compassion does not require you to deny reality or abandon appropriate boundaries.
And if you have been running from God, remember that He already knows the truth you are afraid to confess.
You do not need to manufacture a respectable story before coming to Jesus.
You need to come honestly.
He calls sinners to repentance and promises that those who come to Him will not be cast out (John 6:37).
That is grace.
Not a reward for the impressive.
Not permission to remain unchanged.
Grace that receives the repentant sinner and begins a new life of faith and obedience.
This is why we speak so often about From Scandal to Grace.
Not because every scandal ends in earthly success.
Not because every broken relationship will be restored exactly as we imagine.
Not because the Bible promises a life without consequences.
But because Jesus Christ is able to redeem people whose stories have been marked by shame, failure, injustice, and sin.
He does not erase the truth.
He saves us through the truth of His Gospel.
And He is still transforming lives.
Maybe you have spent years believing that the worst thing that happened to you is the most important thing about you.
Maybe someone labeled you a failure.
A disappointment.
A burden.
A mistake.
Maybe you have repeated those words to yourself so often that they feel like your identity.
But Hagar was more than the way others treated her.
And for those who belong to Christ, the deepest truth about their identity is not found in their shame but in the Savior who redeemed them.
If you are in Christ, you are not beyond His mercy.
You are called to walk in the newness of life He gives.
And if you do not yet know Him, the invitation is open.
Turn from sin.
Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ.
Trust in His death and resurrection.
Come to the One who saves.
Not because you have earned His acceptance.
But because salvation is God's gift of grace through faith, not the achievement of human works (Ephesians 2:8–10).
And if these words are stirring something you have kept hidden, do not rush past that moment.
Perhaps you need to pray.
Perhaps you need to repent.
Perhaps you need to seek help from a trusted believer or pastor.
Perhaps you need to stop pretending that you are fine.
You can begin with a simple, honest prayer:

“Lord Jesus, You know what I have done, what I have suffered, and what I have been hiding. Forgive my sins. Teach me to trust You. Heal what is broken according to Your wisdom. Give me courage to obey You, to seek what is right, and to walk in Your truth. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Help me follow You faithfully. Amen.”
And if this story has reached a place in your heart that you rarely talk about, I want to invite you into a conversation.
You do not have to share private details publicly.
Sometimes a few honest words are enough to let another believer know that someone needs encouragement.
Someone else may be standing at the edge of the very wilderness you have already walked through.
Your testimony may encourage them to turn toward Christ rather than surrender to despair.
There is also someone on your Facebook friends list who may need to read this.
Someone who still attends church but feels spiritually exhausted.
Someone who has stopped praying because disappointment has made hope feel dangerous.
Someone who has never understood why the Gospel is good news for wounded and guilty people alike.
Not merely to increase its reach, but to make biblical encouragement available to someone who might never search for it.
Invite your family, your friends, believers who are struggling, people who have drifted from their faith, and even those who are still searching for answers to follow along.
Because the goal is not simply to produce something emotionally moving.
It is to help people know Jesus Christ more faithfully.
These resources are intended to help believers study Scripture, grow in discernment, strengthen their faith, and develop a deeper walk with Jesus Christ.
And we want to keep making biblical resources accessible.
It can be a meaningful expression of Christian generosity and stewardship.

Scripture encourages believers to support faithful Gospel ministry. Galatians 6:6 speaks of sharing good things with those who teach the Word, while 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should be willing rather than reluctant or compelled.
What matters is a willing heart that desires to honor Christ.
These products can serve as reminders of biblical truth, gifts of encouragement, and opportunities to begin meaningful conversations about faith.
It is participation in a mission that seeks to keep Jesus Christ at the center.
To encourage believers who are weary.
To call wandering hearts back to Scripture.
To help people recognize the seriousness of sin and the wonder of grace.
To remind the broken that redemption is found not in human strength but in the crucified and risen Savior.
Read.
Learn.
Pray.
Help another person discover the free resources.
There are many meaningful ways to participate in spreading the truth of the Gospel, and no one should feel that financial support determines their standing before God.
The mission is Jesus Christ.
And now, before you leave this story, return with me one last time to that spring in the wilderness.
Imagine Hagar standing there.
Dust on her feet.
Fear in her heart.
An uncertain future ahead.
She had no idea how many generations would one day read her story.
She could not have known how often wounded people would return to the words she spoke.
She was simply a woman who had suffered, fled, and been found.
And when she encountered the LORD, she called Him El Ro'i.
The God who sees me.
That confession still matters.
Because the God who saw Hagar is not indifferent to the suffering of His creation.
And the Jesus revealed in the Gospel is not indifferent to sinners in need of salvation.
He came into our broken world.
He bore the cross.
He rose from the dead.
And He calls us to come to Him in repentance and faith.
So if you are tired tonight, do not mistake exhaustion for abandonment.
If you are ashamed, do not assume your sin is beyond the reach of Christ's mercy.
If you have been hurt, do not believe that the cruelty of another person defines your worth.
If you have wandered, hear the invitation of the Savior to return.
And if you are waiting, remember that faithfulness is not always loud.
Sometimes it is simply opening your Bible again.
Praying again.
Confessing again.
Choosing obedience again.
Trusting Jesus with one more day.
Hagar's story began with a household trying to force a promise into existence.
But in the wilderness, the servant learned something no human arrangement could have given her.
God knew her name.
God heard her affliction.
God saw her.
And through the greater story of Scripture, we discover the One who does more than see our brokenness.
Jesus Christ came to redeem sinners and make them new.
You may have been sent into the wilderness by someone else's choices, but your story has never been hidden from the eyes of God.
